title: Stressed, understaffed, and stuck: Examining organizational stressors and job satisfaction in U.S. prisons
abstract: Research Summary This study applies the job demands–resources (JD–R) framework to examine how workplace conditions shape correctional staff emotional stress and job satisfaction. Using survey data from 9656 Florida Department of Corrections employees across 50 state prisons, the study tested whether emotional stress mediates the relationship between workplace demands and job satisfaction and whether perceptions of facility management moderate these effects. Drawing on a larger mixed‐methods project informed by interviews and focus groups with staff, the study examined three organizational demands: officer shortages, a lack of experienced officers, and structural job constraints. A moderated mediation path analysis was used to assess direct, indirect, and conditional relationships. All three demands were associated with higher levels of emotional stress, which, in turn, was linked to lower job satisfaction. In addition, perceptions of effective facility management buffered the negative relationship between emotional stress and job satisfaction and weakened the indirect effects of workplace demands. Policy Implications The findings indicate that addressing correctional workplace stress requires attention to staffing pressures, as well as to broader organizational conditions that shape employee well‐being. Strategies such as targeted recruitment, staffing incentives, and flexible scheduling may help alleviate workforce strain in understaffed facilities. At the same time, the results indicate that leadership quality and organizational support may play important roles in shaping how correctional staff experience emotional stress and job satisfaction. Leadership development initiatives that strengthen supervision, communication, conflict de‐escalation, and mentorship capacity may therefore help improve workplace climate within chronically strained correctional environments. Additional organizational supports, including peer support initiatives, resilience training, and mental health resources tailored to correctional settings, may further assist staff coping and improve institutional functioning.
